Watching the
Rift Move

NISAR radar maps of ground deformation in East Africa

  • Mission: turn satellite radar data into a live map of ground movement along the East African Rift
  • Built to support earthquake, volcano and landslide hazard monitoring
  • Data from NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar); ISRO is the Indian Space Research Organisation
  • Team: E.T
Hi, we're [team]. The East African Rift is slowly pulling Africa apart, and we built a pipeline and a web map that show how the ground is moving there, in centimeters. Our goal is to help people keep watch for earthquake, volcano and landslide hazards.
The problem

A Continent Splitting Apart

  • The African plate is slowly splitting along the East African Rift
  • That brings earthquakes, volcanic activity (for example Afar) and landslides
  • The rift runs from Afar to Mozambique, far too long to watch site by site
  • We need a fast, region-wide view of where the ground is moving
The rift is where Africa is slowly tearing in two, and that is why the region has earthquakes, volcanoes like those in Afar, and landslides. The area is huge, so watching it point by point does not work. Satellites can see all of it.
The method

How Radar Measures Ground Motion

  • NISAR images the same ground again and again
  • InSAR (Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar) compares two radar images taken days apart
  • The difference shows ground moving toward or away from the satellite, in centimeters (LOS = line of sight)
  • Satellites passing ascending and descending see the ground from opposite sides, which lets us separate vertical from east-west motion
[YOUR SCREENSHOT: one real displacement tile]
One granule: red and blue are opposite directions of motion along the line of sight
Think of it as taking the same radar photo twice and subtracting one from the other. Any change is ground movement along the satellite's line of sight, measured in centimeters. Looking from two opposite directions lets us tell up-and-down motion from sideways motion.
The data

The Data and Its Scale

  • Source: NISAR GUNW products (Geocoded UNWrapped interferograms: ready-made ground-motion images) from the Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF)
  • One granule (one frame-sized data file) is about 1 GB and covers about 330 x 330 km, roughly 110,000 km²
  • We took the latest pass of every track over the rift, Afar to Mozambique
  • Total: 339 granules, 176 ascending and 163 descending, plus 17 earlier-pass frames that fill holes (356 processed)

Each NISAR granule is about a gigabyte and covers about 330 by 330 kilometers. We used the newest pass of every track over the rift, which came to 339 granules: 176 ascending and 163 descending. We also processed 17 frames from earlier passes to fill holes in the descending mosaic.
How it works

The Pipeline, Start to Finish

  • Start: either the system spots an earthquake in the USGS (US Geological Survey) feed, or a user types in a request (an area and dates); both set the search box and time window
  • Search and stream: it finds matching NISAR data at ASF and pulls only what it needs
  • Process and mosaic: convert to centimeters of ground motion, filter by signal quality, stitch frames into one regional image
  • Show: a Leaflet web map, linked by a Flask server (Python web server) with live progress

Flask server (Python web server): links the map to the pipeline, with live progress
The pipeline can start two ways: an earthquake report from USGS sets it off automatically, or a user types in an area and dates. Either way, it finds the right radar data, streams just what it needs, turns it into ground-motion maps and stitches them together. The result shows up on a web map, and you can watch progress live.
Smart data access

Stream, Don't Download

  • The usual way: download about 1 GB for every granule
  • Our way: HTTP range requests fetch only the pieces we need
  • Example: about 59 MB of a 981 MB granule, roughly 6%
  • Rough estimate: for 339 granules, that is about 20 GB instead of about 340 GB
Full granule: 981 MB
Streamed: 59 MB (6%)
Both bars use the same scale
Normally you would download a whole gigabyte per granule. We ask the server for just the parts we need, which was about 59 megabytes out of 981, around 6 percent. That is what makes processing a whole rift's worth of data practical.
Putting it together

One Rift-Wide Picture

  • All frames are stitched into one regional image per direction (ascending and descending)
  • Leveling and feathered (smooth) blending hide the frame edges
  • The two directions look from opposite sides, so together they can separate vertical from east-west motion
  • Honest limit: the mosaic mixes passes from different days, so it is a coverage view, not one moment in time

BeforeAfter
Each satellite frame covers only a slice, so we stitch them into one image per direction and blend the edges until the seams disappear. Because the passes are from different days, think of the mosaic as a coverage map, not a snapshot of one moment.
The product

The Interactive Map

  • A Leaflet web map (an open-source mapping library) shows the ground-motion overlays
  • Layers: active faults (GEM, the Global Earthquake Model), USGS earthquakes and critical infrastructure
  • A hazard status: Green, Yellow, Orange or Evacuate
  • A Flask server connects the map to the pipeline, with live progress

What happened

Results, Challenges and Lessons

  • 339 of 339 granules processed: 176 of 176 ascending, 163 of 163 descending (plus 17 earlier-pass frames filling holes)
  • Output: ground-motion rasters in centimeters and two full-rift mosaics

We processed all 339 granules. Along the way we fixed a reader bug, got real parallelism by using processes instead of threads, and corrected map offsets of up to 30 kilometers. [Add one sentence on any real deformation you found, or skip.]
Looking ahead

Impact, Limits and Next Steps

Impact

  • A repeatable way to turn NISAR data into hazard-ready maps, with far less data downloaded

Limits

  • The NISAR data is provisional maturity (early, not final quality)
  • A long smooth color gradient is probably a data ramp (orbital or atmospheric), not real motion, and we have not removed it yet

Next steps

  • Verify the atmospheric (tropospheric) correction and multi-sensor fusion already in our code, then check results against independent measurements

Application in AI

The maps are analysis-ready data (centimeters, with a signal-quality mask) that can feed predictive models, including the risk-scoring and time-to-failure code already in our project. No model is trained yet: that needs more months of data and labelled events.

We want to be upfront: the data is still early-release, and some smooth color trends are likely artifacts, not real movement. Next we will test the atmospheric correction and data fusion we have already coded. Because the maps are analysis-ready, they can also feed predictive models, but we have not trained one yet; that needs more months of data and labelled events. Thank you, and we're happy to take questions.
